beats.vo: So how did Red Lobster end up with a rent bill seventeen times bigger than its shrimp disaster?

visual.brief: Simple number reveal: 17x, with a small caption comparing rent to the shrimp loss.

beats.vo: The answer is a deal. It was signed in 2014, and it involved a restaurant company, a private equity firm, a real estate investment trust,

beats.vo: and, later, the company that supplied the shrimp. This is the postmortem of that deal.

beats.vo: In 1968, a restaurateur named Bill Darden opened a seafood restaurant in Lakeland, Florida.

visual.brief: Archival-style photo of the original 1968 Red Lobster restaurant building in Lakeland, Florida.

beats.vo: He called it Red Lobster, and the idea was simple.

visual.search: vintage Red Lobster restaurant sign 1970s

beats.vo: Seafood, at a price a family could afford, in a place that wasn't a fancy coastal restaurant.

visual.search: family dining casual seafood restaurant 1970s

beats.vo: Two years later, General Mills bought it.

visual.brief: Timeline node appears: 1970, General Mills acquisition.

beats.vo: Under the cereal giant, Red Lobster became a national chain, and in 1995 General Mills spun its restaurant business off as a separate public company,

visual.brief: Timeline continues to 1995 node, Darden Restaurants spin-off.

beats.vo: named after the founder. Darden Restaurants.

visual.brief: Bold wordmark-style card: the new public company's name.

beats.vo: Red Lobster grew into the largest casual dining seafood chain in the United States.

visual.brief: Montage of Red Lobster restaurant exteriors from the 1990s-2010s, chain at scale.
visual.search: Red Lobster restaurant chain exterior multiple locations

beats.vo: Even at the time of its bankruptcy, it served more than sixty-four million customers a year

beats.vo: and bought twenty percent of all North American lobster tails. Darden didn't just run Red Lobster restaurants.

beats.vo: For a large share of them, it owned the land and the buildings too. No landlord. No rent check.

visual.brief: Wide shot of a Red Lobster property — building and land together, no landlord signage, emphasizing ownership.

beats.vo: That real estate sat quietly on the balance sheet, and for a long time nobody outside the company thought much about it.

beats.vo: In 2014, someone did.

beats.vo: By 2013, Red Lobster was in a slow decline. Casual dining was losing customers to fast-casual chains, and seafood costs were volatile.

beats.vo: Darden's stock was lagging its peers. That attracted an activist investor.

visual.brief: Line reveal of Darden's stock price lagging restaurant-sector peers through 2013.

beats.vo: In December 2013, the hedge fund Starboard Value disclosed a 5.6 percent stake in Darden and argued that the company was undervalued.

visual.brief: Bold stat card introducing the activist investor.

beats.vo: Starboard's thesis was about real estate. Darden owned hundreds of restaurant properties, and Starboard believed that value could be unlocked for shareholders,

visual.brief: Aerial/drone-style shot of suburban restaurant real estate parcels — the asset Starboard was pointing at.
visual.search: aerial view suburban restaurant real estate parking lots

beats.vo: ideally in a tax-efficient way, while Darden kept the upside of its restaurants.

visual.brief: Generic corporate office tower exterior, evoking 'tax-efficient value' financial engineering.
visual.search: corporate office tower exterior glass building

beats.vo: Darden's board had a different plan. It wanted to separate Red Lobster from the rest of the company.

visual.brief: Empty boardroom table, generic — the board weighing its plan.
visual.search: empty corporate boardroom table generic

beats.vo: Investors were split. A majority of Darden's shareholders formally asked the board to hold a special meeting before any sale. The board didn't wait.

visual.brief: Highlight the proxy statement line describing shareholders' request for a special meeting that the board bypassed.

beats.vo: On May 16, 2014, Darden announced it was selling Red Lobster, the restaurants and the real estate together,

beats.vo: to the private equity firm Golden Gate Capital.

visual.brief: Clean name card for the buyer.

visual.brief: Highlight the exact proxy-statement sentence stating gross vs. net proceeds.

doc.quote: to Golden Gate Capital for $2.1 billion in cash

beats.vo: At the same moment, Golden Gate signed a second agreement.

visual.brief: Quick transition shot — a second signature line, second contract, implying a second, simultaneous deal.
visual.search: business contract signature page close up

beats.vo: It would sell Red Lobster's real estate to a real estate investment trust called American Realty Capital Properties, for one point five billion dollars.

visual.brief: Deal-flow diagram: Darden → Golden Gate ($2.1B) → ARCP ($1.5B real estate), boxes and arrows animating in.

beats.vo: This is called a sale-leaseback. A company sells the buildings it owns, then signs a long-term lease to keep operating in them.

visual.brief: Simple abstract diagram animation: a building icon splits into 'sold' (deed changes hands) and 'leased back' (arrow looping back into the same building), no people, no real logos.
visual.prompt: Minimalist flat-icon animation: a building outline, an arrow showing it being sold away, then a second arrow looping back labeled lease, clean vector style, brand colors paper background ink lines red accent

beats.vo: It gets a big check today. In exchange, it pays rent forever after.

visual.brief: Close-up of hands (unidentifiable) exchanging a generic bank check across a table.

beats.vo: Here is what that did to the math.

visual.brief: Section bumper before the math breakdown.

beats.vo: Golden Gate agreed to pay roughly two point one billion for Red Lobster.

visual.brief: Bar grows in: $2.1B price paid.

beats.vo: It agreed, at the same time, to sell the buildings for one point five billion.

visual.brief: Second bar grows in beside the first: $1.5B real estate sold.

beats.vo: That leaves roughly six hundred million dollars for the restaurant business itself, before fees and financing.

beats.vo: Starboard ran the same numbers from Darden's side and was furious.

visual.brief: Generic activist-investor office setting, papers and a phone on a desk, no identifiable people.

beats.vo: In its proxy fight later that summer, it argued that Darden could have captured the real estate value itself, tax-free,

visual.search: proxy statement legal document close up pages

beats.vo: and that the deal valued the actual restaurant business at about one hundred million dollars, less than one year of its earnings.

doc.quote: just $100 million in value for Red Lobster’s operating business, or less than 1x EBITDA

beats.vo: Starboard called it a fire sale.

visual.brief: Bold red stamp-style card punctuating Starboard's characterization.

beats.vo: For Red Lobster, the restaurant chain, the deal changed one thing permanently.

beats.vo: The logic is well known in the industry.

visual.brief: Continue on financial district b-roll, wide establishing shot.

beats.vo: Selling the real estate reduces how much of the buyer's own money is tied up in the deal.

visual.prompt: Minimalist flat-icon animation, a stack of coins shrinking with a downward arrow labeled equity, clean vector style, paper background ink lines red accent

beats.vo: The property investor gets a long, predictable stream of rent. And if the restaurants perform, everyone does well.

visual.prompt: Minimalist flat-icon animation, a steady horizontal stream of coin icons flowing into a simple building icon, clean vector style, paper background ink lines red accent

beats.vo: The risk sits with the tenant. Rent doesn't care whether customers show up. It escalates in good years and bad ones.

beats.vo: A sale-leaseback isn't a bad tool.

visual.brief: Neutral, non-judgmental transition card.

beats.vo: It makes sense when the real estate is worth more to a property investor than it is sitting inside an operating company,

visual.brief: Commercial real estate photography, 'for lease' framing, neutral tone.

beats.vo: when the cash goes somewhere that earns more than the rent costs,

visual.brief: Continue: cash flowing through a generic ledger/spreadsheet on a laptop screen.

beats.vo: and when the business is healthy enough to cover that rent comfortably in a bad year, not just a good one.

visual.search: busy successful restaurant interior dining

beats.vo: What would worry an advisor here is the bundling.

visual.brief: Section bumper flagging the analytical caveat.
